channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: News from Special Collections & Archives: New Finding Aids Site is Live!
item.description: ZSR Library, Wake Forest University: “With our new site, we are proud to have incorporated some new features that we hope will make for a more efficient and enjoyable researching experience, providing access to to the 2,000+ archival collections stewarded by Z. Smith Reynolds Library Special Collections & Archives.”

item.title: Introducing PixelMeter: The Reviews Aggregator for Cameras, Lenses, Smartphones, and More
item.description: PetaPixel: “PetaPixel has announced PixelMeter, the camera industry’s first review aggregator platform. PixelMeter collects reviews from across the landscape and condenses the opinions into a single, standardized score so photographers can see the best gear at a glance.”

item.title: YouTube is reworking the Home page with Custom Feeds and quicker access to Subscriptions
item.description: DigitalTrends: “YouTube is changing how its Home page works, giving viewers more control over what shows up there and making some of the app’s most-used sections easier to reach. Custom Feeds are now replacing the existing topic chips for eligible users, while YouTube is also testing a redesigned top bar on mobile that moves Subscriptions closer to the Home feed.”

item.title: YouTube now gets twice as much watch time on U.S. TVs as any other platform
item.description: Tubefilter: “…in the August 2026 edition of The Gauge, YouTube had an especially strong showing. It claimed its biggest watch time share ever — 15.8% — as streaming platforms accounted for nearly half of the TV screen traffic recorded by Nielsen.”

item.title: ‘I’m 96 and have 15 million followers’: The grannies taking over TikTok
item.description: BBC: “Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties. The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks.”

item.title: Hallowen 2K26 – Some Old Web 1.0 Horror Fansites
item.description: Brandon’s Journal: “Recently, I took a look back at some old abandoned Scream fansites I found online. I had fun conducting a little internet archaeology and discovering these old works of love before they disappear forever. Sadly, Web 1.0 is dying as the internet continues to grow, and I guess I feel a certain obligation to keep some of that spirit alive. That’s what inspired me to create this post to begin with, and I feel like paying homage to those who came before is only right.”

item.title: On ‘Settle In,’ Kathryn Jezer-Morton and Geoff Bennett discuss social media’s impact
item.description: PBS NewsHour: “Social media lets us share our lives with family, friends, and strangers. But how do people decide what to post, what to leave out, and what do those decisions say about them? On ‘Settle In,’ Geoff Bennett discusses that with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of ‘The Story of Your Life,’ a new book about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell.”

item.title: Internet trade group sues California over social media warning labels
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “NetChoice, a trade association whose members include Meta, Google and TikTok, sued California on Thursday to stop a state law requiring social media platforms to display warning labels for users under 18 about the mental health risks of social media use. NetChoice said in a complaint filed in Los Angeles federal court that the law, which goes into effect on Jan. 1, violates the First Amendment prohibition against compelled speech.”

item.title: How a Legal Backlash Against Big Tech Is Forcing Big Changes
item.description: New York Times: “For decades, tech giants grew at breakneck speeds as Congress struggled to keep pace with the consequences of the companies’ rapidly booming businesses. But a new de facto regulatory regime has emerged over the past year as courts clobber the biggest internet companies. And for the first time, their product designs and advertising models — which critics say treat users as products — are costing the companies serious money.”

item.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
item.description: Ars Technica: “A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: CDC uses new tool to track flu as season picks up ahead of schedule
item.description: WRDW: “Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz says a new tool is helping identify spikes in flu cases as flu season picks up months ahead of schedule and a new mutation is causing a rise in cases. The tool is designed to empower communities and individuals to know how best to protect themselves.”

item.title: Preserving More Than the Web: Building an Archive of Online Resources for Preservation and Conservation
item.description: Library of Congress: “I am a Preservation Librarian in the Conservation Division. Part of my role is ensuring that conservators and preservation scientists have access to the resources they need for their work, including new scholarly publications. As more of those resources became available only online, I realized we needed to preserve access for the future, which led to creating the Preservation and Conservation Web Archive. I am the Collection Leader, and I’ve researched the field and worked with colleagues across the Conservation Division to identify resources to include in the collection.”

item.title: a big dataset on the history of American hotels.
item.description: Today I learned about an archivist named Larry R. Paul who has created “The Hotel Database is long-term research project that details, when known, the following information for more than 43,000 hotels in the United States, spanning nearly 100 years: Name – Location – Construction, Closure, Conversion, Destruction – Architect/Builder – Owner/Operators – Cost – Architectural Syle/Features/Additions – Floors/Rooms – Notes on China Service – Restaurants/Lounges/Coffee Shops, Ballroom. A primary source of research has been Hotel Red Books – from 1904 through 1969 – and in many ways the database can be thought of as the information from 65 years of HRBs compiled under one cover.”

item.title: Bluesky adds iPad support in latest feature update
item.description: Engadget: “Bluesky rolled out several features in its latest update, notably beta testing support for iPads…. Another update is aimed at self-promotion. Bluesky users can now put links to external platforms at the top of their profiles.”

item.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
item.description: Ars Technica: “eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.”

item.title: The Epstein Files Produce an Unlikely Weapon for the Houthi Messaging Wars
item.description: New York Times: “The Houthis control much of Yemen. Their communications show a profound awareness of news that their sworn enemies generate. They are willing to deploy the information in many forms — songs, videos, speeches, statements, influencer posts and more — to build support and target foes, including Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognized Yemeni government they are fighting. They portray themselves as defenders of Islam against corrupt foreign influences. Now, the group has stepped up its messaging efforts, after Yemen’s civil war reignited this summer amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.”

item.title: Hundreds of Protestors Descend on Meta Corporate Office Depicting Zuck as the Devil
item.description: Futurism: “Meta’s corporate offices in São Paulo are the site of ongoing protests against election interference in the crucial national run-off elections in Brazil. Hundreds of protestors rallied at the company’s offices on Tuesday, carrying effigies mocking Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg as the devil incarnate, Venezuelan publication TeleSur reported.”

item.title: PHP Foundation ‘under-funded’ with one full-time staff member, director says
item.description: Reuters: “The discovery of two ​serious flaws in PHP this week set off a global scramble to ‌keep websites safe from hackers, showing just how critical the three-decade-old open-source programming language, opens new tab is to the internet. Yet the nonprofit foundation that supports PHP, which may underpin up to 70% of sites globally, operates on ​a shoestring budget.” Silicon Valley companies have billions and billions in cash reserves but can’t be bothered to support the software they’re built on.

item.title: Capcom data breach confirmed: More than 11 million accounts impacted
item.description: Mashable: “Do you play video games like Street Fighter, Resident Evil, or Monster Hunter online? If so, you probably have a Capcom ID — and you should know that there has been a major data breach that has affected millions of accounts. Capcom, the developer of the aforementioned titles, posted a notice on Thursday informing users of a major data breach affecting more than 11 million accounts.”

item.title: The EPA Is Quietly Killing its Web Archive
item.description: Mother Jones: “In a little-noticed webpage update, the Environmental Protection Agency has announced a plan to decommission its online web archive at the end of the year, a move that would wipe tens of thousands of publicly available environmental resources from the web. The discreet banner notice comes in stark contrast to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin’s recent public takedowns of the agency’s power plant pollution standards and federal methane regulatory system.”

item.title: Researchers Pinpoint the Exact Location of First Ever Photo of a Human
item.description: PetaPixel: “At first glance, Daguerre’s image View of the Boulevard du Temple seems to show a deserted street, but two individuals were captured during the four- to five-minute-long exposure time.. These two people — a shoeshine boy and his client — inadvertently became the first two human subjects to appear in a photograph.”

item.title: Free-entry museums to benefit from new business rates policy after landmark tribunal ruling
item.description: Museums Journal: “Free-to-enter museums and galleries across England will benefit from significant reductions in their business rates valuations following a landmark legal case won by London’s Natural History Museum earlier this year. In an update to sector stakeholders, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) confirmed that the Valuation Office (VO) would no longer use a notional receipts approach to value free-to-enter museums for business rates purposes.” Good evening, Internet….

item.title: New Department of Public Health dashboard brings local overdose data to Connecticut communities
item.description: Connecticut Department of Public Health: “The Connecticut Department of Public Health (DPH) today launched the Report on Connecticut Unintentional Overdose Deaths. This new online dashboard shows local data on deaths caused by drug overdoses. It is updated each month. People can view data for the state, their town, or their region and see how patterns change over time.”

item.title: Twitch’s new Stream Recap turns missed livestreams into highlight reels you can watch in minutes
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Have you ever missed the chance to watch your favorite streamer going live? This is why Twitch has launched Stream Recaps, a new feature that bundles the best clips from a livestream into one highlight reel. You can now catch key moments in minutes instead of replaying hours of video.”

item.title: Court lifts block on Georgia law that restricts children’s access to social media
item.description: The Current Georgia: “Georgia can enforce a 2024 state law that seeks to limit social media companies’ access to children under a new ruling by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The Protecting Georgia’s Children on Social Media Act passed the General Assembly with broad bipartisan support, but an organization representing online platforms sued and secured a preliminary injunction last year.”

item.title: New iPhone Camera App Makes You Wait To See Your Photos
item.description: PetaPixel: “[Dennis] Berti’s new app, WorthWait Camera, lets users capture 24 or 36 shots per ‘roll,’ then wait 24 hours to see them. It’s designed to recreate the feeling of waiting for photos and not knowing what was captured until the film was developed.”

item.title: GridCraft is the open-source Excel clone for Linux I’ve been waiting for
item.description: ZDNet: “You might be thinking that this is simply a rebranded MS Excel that runs on top of an interpretation or abstraction layer, but that is not the case. Like the other ArtCraft apps, GridCraft runs natively on whatever OS you are using (Linux, FreeBSD, MacOS, or Windows). And because these apps were written in Rust, they are blazingly fast.”

item.title: Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic.
item.description: Ars Technica: “Smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue sending data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints after users opt out of tracking in the devices’ settings, according to research published on Monday. The paper from Northeastern University researchers points to potential privacy violations from some of the biggest TV brands.”

item.title: When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data
item.description: NiemanLab: “Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments…. How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data.”

item.title: New global database provides a fuller picture of the elements that make up plant life
item.description: Texas A&M: “[Harrison] Coker and an international team have now helped establish that baseline. In a study and global meta-analysis published in ACS Environmental Au, they compiled measurements from 5,474 plant samples across 73 countries, covering 52 elements, 21 climate classes and 26 soil groups. The resulting global database provides a more comprehensive picture of plant elemental composition, including dozens of elements beyond the familiar nutrients typically associated with plant growth.”

item.title: When crises disappear from view: The growing humanitarian data drought
item.description: International Food Policy Research Institute: “During a time of growing, compounding risks to the global food system—including ongoing conflicts, the most severe El Niño in decades, and disruptions to global trade—in too many places, humanitarian data are disappearing. Government budget cuts, shrinking development assistance, and competing priorities are eroding key streams of data on food security and a range of related issues. This humanitarian data drought is an emerging challenge that threatens to worsen existing crises and possibly create new ones. It demands action to safeguard critical humanitarian data streams. Without fresh data, people in crisis become harder to see, harder to reach, and all too easy to overlook.”

item.title: Deep-Sea Octopus Discovers Laser Pointers, Immediately Gets the Zoomies
item.description: Geeks Are Sexy: “During the E/V Nautilus expedition in the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, ROV Hercules spotted a camouflaged octopus on the seafloor that promptly developed a severe case of the zoomies, chasing the ROV’s green scaling lasers across the sand.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Explore the history of View-Master 3D through a Santa Maria resident’s new documentary
item.description: New-to-me, from the Santa Maria Sun: “Dave Machin’s hobby collecting View-Master 3D toys started by chance when he picked one up at an antique shop in San Luis Obispo. He clicked through travel reels of destinations like Yosemite, Chicago, and Miami…. He manually converted his stockpile of vintage viewers and reels into a large online database to occupy his mind during the pandemic. Then, an idea for a project sparked.”

item.title: A Former Radiologist Is Building an Online Archive of Lost St. Louis Restaurants — Here’s How It’s Bringing People Together
item.description: People: “A retired radiologist is mapping the lost restaurants of St. Louis. Harley Hammerman has created Lost Tables, an archival collection of the lost restaurants of the Missouri city, featuring a website and a Facebook group with over 20,000 members.”

item.title: 40,000 more 9/11 records released as questions linger over toxic air warnings
item.description: AMNY: “Mayor Zohran Mamdani‘s administration released on Wednesday another 40,000 documents related to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, adding to a growing public archive of records that survivors and first responders spent years fighting to access.”

item.title: Google Docs finally learned Markdown
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Google Docs now natively supports editing .md and .markdown files. This means you can upload and edit your Markdown files directly from Google Drive without needing to convert them first.”

item.title: Google Maps changed its default voice to be more ‘natural.’ People hate it
item.description: CBC: “Google Maps has changed its default voice for directions — you know, the one that tells you where to turn and how many kilometres until the off-ramp — and it’s safe to say many people are not fans of the new mouthpiece directing them from Point A to Point B.”

item.title: Archives Partnership Trust Launches New Programs to Expand Educator Access and Enhance Classroom Instruction of New York’s Primary Source Materials
item.description: New York State Education Department: “The New York State Education Department and Archives Partnership Trust’s RDL Gardiner Foundation Educational Resource Center for New York State History today announced two new educational initiatives that will expand access to New York’s historical records and further empower the state’s educators to use primary source materials in the classroom.”

item.title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
item.description: Ars Technica: “Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.”

item.title: Atlanta social media influencer indicted in $4 million SNAP fraud scheme
item.description: WABE: “The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia announced Wednesday that social media personality Mercedes Reshard New, also known as ‘Shawty Dred,’ has been arrested on federal charges after allegedly obtaining more than $4 million in fraudulent SNAP benefits.”

item.title: Some final words on Foursquare
item.description: Dennis Crowley: “After 17 years, FSQ’s ending has been written. Some thoughts on our final years, an effort to honor the team who helped build & maintain FSQ’s legacy, and my attempt to finally get some closure.”

item.title: Become Part of the Legacy of Abolitionist and Educator, Myrtilla Miner
item.description: Library of Congress: “In 1851, more than a decade before the Emancipation Proclamation was issued, the School for Colored Girls opened in Washington, D.C. with the mission of training Black women educators. The institution was the first of its kind in the District and only the fourth in the nation. Today, the Library of Congress and the By the People volunteer transcription program invite you to celebrate the life and legacy of its courageous and barrier-breaking founder, Myrtilla Miner (1815-1864).” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: October 2026 Crawl Archive Now Available
item.description: Common Crawl: “The crawl archive for October 2026 is now available. The data was crawled between October 5th and October 18th, and contains 2.16 billion web pages (or 371.19 TiB of uncompressed content). Page captures are from 41.4 million hosts or 34.3 million registered domains and include 830.1 million new URLs, not visited in any of our prior crawls.”

item.title: Motorsports Hall of Fame of America Launches Historic Joseph Freeman Collection
item.description: Motorsports Hall of Fame of America: “The Joseph Freeman Collection spans over a century of racing, starting in the 1890s, and includes Indy cars, Sprint cars, Midgets, Formula 1, Sports Cars, Stock Cars, Motorcycles, Off-Road, Powerboats, Land Speed and other categories captured by nearly three dozen of the world’s finest motorsports photographers.”

item.title: AskChem: A New Search Engine for Chemistry Research
item.description: NYU Center for Data Science: “A chemist choosing how to make a molecule may need to compare reaction conditions and results scattered across dozens of papers. NYU Courant Computer Science PhD candidate Bing Yan and colleagues developed AskChem to make those individual findings searchable, with each result linked to evidence in its source paper.”

item.title: Google Chrome’s new early warning system could help you spot scam sites
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Anyone who has used Google Chrome has probably seen the red warning screen when they click a suspicious link or try to visit a potentially dangerous website. Google is now beefing up this warning system by adding a new layer that will flag websites that seem fishy, even when Safe Browsing does not have enough confidence to classify them as outright dangerous.”

item.title: Should parents be wary of Silicon Valley’s influence in schools?
item.description: Harvard Gazette: “…leading technologists and executives have been drawn to classrooms in recent decades as laboratories, market opportunities, and above all, problems waiting to be solved — whether with computers, software, or AI chatbots, according to Natasha Singer. Since 2013, Singer has watched those efforts closely as a New York Times tech reporter. She found them at best quixotic or naive and at worst insidious, threatening to deprive young Americans of their ability to think critically about some of the world’s largest companies.”

item.title: H3 Podcast Crew Cuts Ties With Ethan Klein After Hila Klein Says He Has Been Having an Affair
item.description: Variety: “The ‘H3 Podcast,’ the show co-hosted by Ethan and Hila Klein, is on indefinite hiatus after Hila said he has been having an affair for the last six months and that the couple has separated.”

item.title: Manuel Otto, German video game creator, dies in apparent livestreamed suicide
item.description: NBC News: “German video game designer and influencer Manuel Otto apparently died by suicide while he was livestreaming on Twitch, according to the streaming platform and his colleagues. He was 30.”

item.title: Hegseth warns prediction market bets warp military judgment, endanger troops
item.description: Ars Technica: “Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo warning military personnel against using nonpublic information to make bets on prediction markets, saying the wagers could give important clues to enemy countries.”

item.title: Former Florida congressional candidate faces felony charges over online threats
item.description: MS NOW: “Two days after Elijah Manley came in third place in the hotly contested August Democratic primary in Florida’s 20th Congressional District, he allegedly told two women on Facebook he would ‘make your life a living hell’ and ‘cut your fucking head off’ if they did not vote for [Angie] Nixon, according to an arrest affidavit reviewed by MS NOW.”

item.title: Swiss former president tackles Nazi-era and colonial loot in museums
item.description: SwissInfo: “A new Swiss commission, led by former president Simonetta Sommaruga, is now accepting claims for Nazi-looted art and colonial-era cultural property. It will review disputed cases and issue recommendations. Sommaruga spoke to Swissinfo about its mission and priorities.”

item.title: Africa moves to establish raw materials database
item.description: Punch (Nigeria): “The Raw Materials Research and Development Council has said African countries are working towards establishing a continental database of raw materials to attract investment, improve access to information and promote research and value addition.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: AI reads centuries-old handwriting to reveal Britain’s vast historic shipping trade
item.description: University of Southampton: “Historians have created a first-of-its-kind online interactive map, using data from hundreds of thousands of pages of centuries-old port records to chart Britain’s growth into a dominant global trading nation. The University of Southampton project used artificial intelligence to transform information from delicate handwritten ‘port books’ into an enormous database of Britain’s merchant shipping past.”

item.title: Milestone met: WA Legends presses on
item.description: Sounder at Heart: “The fact that Washington State Legends of Soccer is marking its 10th anniversary this month is something to celebrate. Most small businesses fail before their eighth trip around the sun. Adding a pandemic into the equation won’t help.”

item.title: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
item.description: Associated Press: “While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex’s virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia’s judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access.”

item.title: My USB drive carries Wikipedia and a library that doesn’t need Wi-Fi
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I’ve used flash drives for years as glorified pockets for files I’ll probably forget about. Then I loaded Kiwix onto my PC, pointed it at a 16GB stick, and the drive finally got a real job. It now holds a slice of Wikipedia, a Project Gutenberg collection, and room for more reference material that still opens when Windows insists there’s no internet connection. I already knew about plenty of clever ways to repurpose old USB drives, but carrying around an offline reference shelf has become one of my favorites.”

item.title: Wales plans £400k deal for national online family history service
item.description: Public Technology: “The National Library of Wales has revealed plans to invest a six-figure sum in an online service for citizens to investigate their family history. The library – which holds charity status and operates as an arm’s-length body of the Welsh Government – has published a procurement notice alerting potential suppliers that it ‘is seeking to appoint a single service provider to deliver an online family history service’.”

item.title: Some Google Home Speakers downloading massive amounts of data in the background
item.description: 9to5 Google: “In my case, a Google Home Speaker that has not been used in the past day for voice commands or media streaming consumed 17 GB of data in 24 hours. At 3 a.m. PT, it downloaded 9.99 GB. Given the timing, this could be related to failed attempts to download device firmware.”

item.title: UpdraftPlus WordPress Plugin Security Breach Enables Backdoor Attacks
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “A security breach affecting UpdraftPlus, a WordPress backup plugin installed on over 3 million websites, enabled attackers to install malicious plugins and create unauthorized administrator accounts. The attack exploited compromised UpdraftCentral connection keys, allowing attackers to take control of connected WordPress websites without needing a username or password.”

item.title: German court calls Google aerial imagery ‘spying’
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “A German court on Tuesday ruled Google is breaking Germany’s strict privacy laws by showing people’s properties on its Google Earth and Google Maps services. The Frankfurt Regional Court equated Google’s satellite and aerial 3D imagery services to ‘spying’ when it displays pictures of property without getting permission.”

item.title: Smart glasses will be banned in all Victorian schools
item.description: The Daily Aus: “Victoria will ban all students across the state from using smart glasses in schools and camps. The ban, announced by the Labor Government ahead of the state’s November election, will build on its existing statewide ban on mobile phones in schools. The Coalition also supports the ban. The new rules will prohibit smart glasses in public, independent and Catholic schools from the start of the 2027 school year.”

item.title: Study Highlights Need for Policymakers to Look at Digital Policies as Part of Energy, Climate Planning
item.description: North Carolina State University: “A new study underscores the extent to which digital policies cannot be separated from energy policies. The research evaluates the relationship between information communication technologies and carbon dioxide emissions, and finds that the variables they used as proxies for digitalization were associated with increased emissions.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: EFF Launches Guide to Help Parents and Youth Protect Privacy Online
item.description: EFF: “EFF’s guide is about helping parents explore their concerns and identify the threats their children face – like trusting AI chatbots or sharing personal information with strangers – and then determine steps they and their children can take to mitigate those risks while still using the games, educational materials, and communication platforms that help them grow. The guide also compiles links to parental control setup documentation for a variety of popular devices and platforms, and advises parents on quick, easy tasks they can perform to advance their children’s online privacy.”

item.title: New archive launched to help preserve Scotland’s historic castles
item.description: The Herald (Scotland): “The archive currently includes the Robert and Nicholas Bogdan collection, with further collections being catalogued and digitised. Some material is already available online. The Scottish Castles Association hopes the archive will become a freely accessible resource for anyone interested in Scotland’s castles, bringing together photographs, drawings, research and records previously held across private and institutional collections.”

item.title: Video Game History Foundation Shares Never-Before-Seen Images from Golden Age of Japanese Video Game Culture
item.description: Video Game History Foundation: “The Video Game History Foundation (VGHF) is excited to add a brand new collection to its ever-growing Digital Library, this time peering back into the boom era of the Japanese video game industry with the aid of numerous photos from resident journalist Colin Williamson.”

item.title: 5.0: A closer look
item.description: Mastodon Blog: “October is here, and it’s almost time for Mastodon’s 5.0 release! We announced our plans for big changes in an early preview back in August. In this companion article, we’re hoping to shed light on some of the decisions behind this major UI overhaul.”

item.title: Publishers urged to delete Facebook and Instagram accounts over T&Cs change
item.description: Press Gazette: “Campaign group Movement for an Open Web is preparing a legal challenge via the European Commission and UK Competition and Markets Authority. Director James Rosewell said: ‘The harm is imminent and irreversible once content has been ingested into models. Timing matters.'”

item.title: Tech giants target spending on Florida’s state-level elections
item.description: Politico: “Tech firms are donating to Democrats and Republican candidates alike, buying scores of mailers and ads on top of making campaign contributions in the upcoming November midterms races. They’re also funneling tens of thousands of dollars — a meager sum compared to statewide races, but notable at the statehouse level — through a dizzying network of political committees that support Republican leaders in the state Legislature and lawmakers who had a hand in artificial intelligence legislation last session.”

item.title: Digital archive helps Sydney’s southern Lebanese community preserve villages now in rubble
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “People with southern Lebanese heritage were invited to bring photographs and videos of their ancestral villages, many of which have been damaged or destroyed by the Israeli military over the past six months. A recent analysis by The New York Times found that 48 out of the 60 villages in occupied areas of southern Lebanon had been mostly levelled, including schools, mosques and businesses.”

item.title: Hooked on YouTube
item.description: NBC News: “Schools wanted educational videos. Students got clickbait. A first-of-its-kind analysis reveals how students are drawn into a platform that keeps them scrolling during class.”

item.title: New Greece law bans social media for under-15s
item.description: AFP: “Greece’s parliament passed a law Friday banning children under 15 from social media, joining a growing number of countries imposing curbs on young people’s use of the apps.”

item.title: Attorney General Neronha sues Meta for fraudulent advertisements
item.description: State of Rhode Island: “Attorney General Peter F. Neronha today filed a lawsuit against Meta for allegedly failing to curtail advertisements for fraudulent products and financial scams on its platforms, despite representing to the public that it engages in sophisticated efforts to prevent such ads.”

item.title: Judge Orders Meta to Name Employees Who Approved Torrenting Anna’s Archive and LibGen
item.description: TorrentFreak: “Meta will have to name the people who greenlit its torrenting of pirated books. A federal magistrate judge has ordered the company to identify everyone who approved sourcing books from LibGen and Anna’s Archive. This goes beyond the employees who ran the downloads and includes whoever decided whether to seed the books to others.”

item.title: Search Share Fell To 12% For North American Publishers: Chartbeat
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Search engines accounted for 12% of all page views at North American publishers in Chartbeat’s network, based on the data found within the analytics firm’s Q3’26 Audience Report, which was released October 15th, 2026, whereas they represented 21% of page views as reported in the firm’s Q3’25 report.”

item.title: V&A launches full digital archive dating back to 2003, available to all members
item.description: ArtDaily: “The complete archive of V&A Magazine is now digitally available to all V&A members for the first time. Archived since Spring 2003, the collection comprises over 70 issues and explores some of the most significant developments to occur within the museum over the past 20 years. Digital access is included in a V&A membership, and is also available through individual and institutional subscriptions via Exact Editions.”

item.title: Archives of Michigan releases collection highlighting Michigan’s 1961-1962 Constitutional Convention
item.description: State of Michigan: “Today, the Michigan Department of Technology, Management & Budget (DTMB) announced that the Archives of Michigan has released a collection highlighting the preservation of Michigan’s 1961-1962 Constitutional Convention, which was made possible by a $50,000 grant through the Council on Library and Information Resources’ (CLIR) Recordings at Risk program.”

item.title: Critical PHP Security Release
item.description: WordPress: “Due to the critical severity of the issues, site owners are encouraged to immediately update their installations of PHP. Your web host may already be working to update PHP and put web application firewall (WAF) rules in place to mitigate the vulnerabilities, but you should still check for updates from your web host and, if necessary, update PHP as soon as possible.”

item.title: Meta tells Brazil’s electoral court it gives equal treatment to Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
item.description: Associated Press: “Tech giant Meta said on Tuesday it has complied with an order of Brazil’s electoral court for it to give equal treatment in its platforms to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and opposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of the Oct. 25 runoff for the nation’s top job.”

item.title: Russia launched covert influence campaign to undermine US candidates supportive of Ukraine, lawmakers say
item.description: Politico: “The Russian government has launched a covert online influence campaign to sway public opinion and undermine both Democrats and Republicans sympathetic to Ukraine ahead of the midterms, two key Democratic lawmakers warned Wednesday.”

item.title: These 6 retro sites let you relive the glory days of 2000s Flash games
item.description: Engadget: “Adobe ended support for Flash Player on December 31, 2020. This was due to a changing landscape where standards like HTML5 reduced the need for plugins like Flash, which suffered from security vulnerabilities that couldn’t be sufficiently addressed over the years…. But that doesn’t mean content built with Flash is gone forever. You can thankfully still play Flash games in 2026 using websites that run the original programs, most of them using an open-source Flash emulator called Ruffle.”

item.title: What is PHP and how serious is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns?
item.description: The Guardian: “Website owners faced millions of attempts to exploit a serious security vulnerability in their programming language, it has emerged, triggering a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem. The newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that underpins most websites, allows hackers to carry out cyber-attacks and steal data if not fixed. What were the vulnerabilities and why did they affect so many sites?”

item.title: Norway targets ‘harmful’ social media, games with under-16 ban
item.description: Reuters: “Norway’s planned social media ban for children will include provisions targeting ‘harmful platforms’, the government said on Monday, naming messaging and gaming ​services Roblox, Snapchat and TikTok among those affected.”

item.title: Personal information for 7M California students stolen following hack
item.description: EdSource: “The personal information of about 7 million California students has been stolen following a hack of the organization responsible for administering the state’s Smarter Balanced Assessments and English proficiency exams, Politico reported.”

item.title: Accident Or Not, The No Kings Takedown Is Why You Shouldn’t Rent Your Megaphone From Zuck
item.description: Techdirt: “This past weekend was the latest in an ongoing series of (massive) ‘No Kings’ protests held around the country (and in some cases around the globe). The latest one was part of a ‘get out the (early) vote’ campaign to make sure people are voting in the upcoming midterm elections. And, in the middle of it, suddenly it was reported that the No Kings Instagram account was suspended for about an hour, with admin access locked out for a few more hours.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Meta Muse exposes users’ personal and business secrets when they share conversations
item.description: Ars Technica: “Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.”

item.title: Data center real estate is getting hard to find
item.description: Politico: “backlash to large data centers for artificial intelligence is rewriting the rules. Instead of ramping up tax incentives, 16 state legislatures have considered outright bans on their development. As the glut in projects strains U.S. electrical grids and voters from both parties increasingly sour on the bulky facilities, developers are rethinking what they really need.”

item.title: Data centers can’t be stopped, but good policy is needed, NDSU researcher says
item.description: North Dakota Monitor: “There’s no way of stopping the development of data centers and artificial intelligence, a North Dakota State University researcher said Wednesday, adding that attempts to slow development would only push it to other areas.”

item.title: Scoop: Unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts
item.description: Axios: “Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.”

item.title: Canva releases its first image generation model
item.description: TechCrunch: “Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.”

item.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
item.description: The Guardian: “Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.”

item.title: A Denver Chinese restaurant owner wanted a better name for a bun. So she turned to ChatGPT.
item.description: Denver Post: “Like [Nina] Zhang, local restaurateurs are using ChatGPT and similar chatbots to experiment with their recipes, design promotional fliers, manage inventory and handle workplace conflicts. The tool has helped them run their restaurants more efficiently at a time when many in the industry are making razor-thin margins, they said.”

item.title: KATU probes alleged ‘deepfake’ as cached images show upside-down flag behind Nafisa Fai
item.description: KATU: “KATU is investigating the controversy surrounding an alleged ‘deepfake’ video of Washington County Commissioner Nafisa Fai speaking at an event in Minnesota in front of an upside-down American flag. Fai is running against fellow Washington County Commissioner Pam Treece to become chair of the County Board of Commissioners.”

item.title: IMF Warns That AI Bubble Could Take Down the Entire World Economy
item.description: Futurism: “Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for years. And now the International Monetary Fund is the latest to sound the alarm. In its Global Financial Stability Report published last week, the global financial institution warned that markets everywhere are increasingly at the mercy of precarious AI investments.”

item.title: Florida lawyer referred for possible discipline over filing that judges called ‘AI slop’
item.description: Reuters: “A Florida appeals court on Wednesday referred a lawyer to the Florida bar for possible professional discipline after finding her filings in a case bore hallmarks ​of generative AI output that the panel of judges called ‘AI slop.'”

item.title: Customer Service Chatbots Must Be Stopped
item.description: New York Times: “It’s easy to dismiss these exhausting mazes of chatbots, robocalls, irrelevant pop-ups and consent forms as the routine irritations of life lived on tiny screens. But taken together, these episodes can amount to something much larger — delayed medical care, denied insurance coverage, predatory subscription practices and scams that cost Americans an estimated $119 billion a year. Now, artificial intelligence is starting to make a bad situation worse.”

item.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
item.description: The Conversation: “I’m a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, where I study free speech policy. In two reports published in 2025 and 2026, my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they often use existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say.”

item.title: AI is shaking up the field of mathematics. But what comes next?
item.description: NPR: “Mathematicians are struggling to figure out what to do with a flood of new results from artificial intelligence. As NPR’s Geoff Brumfiel reports, a release by the company OpenAI is shaping up to be just a massive homework assignment.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: AI-built database of 378,000 English word families reveals how morphology shapes children’s reading
item.description: Scienmag: “A team of reading researchers has unveiled what they describe as the largest morphological database of English ever constructed, and used it to map, with unprecedented scope, the word-building patterns that children encounter as they learn to read.”

item.title: Techno-Optimism Archive
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds, apparently launched in late April: the “Techno-Optimism Archive traces the long history of hype surrounding new technologies….explore moments when the next big invention was supposed to solve the world’s problems.”

item.title: Arc browser is shutting down in December. Long live, ya trailblazer
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Arc browser is shutting down on December 22, following a long spell of maintenance-only work as the company behind it moves forward with its successor, Dia. Earlier today, The Browser Company announced that the beloved web browser will ride into the sunset in two months, but will continue development of the Dia browser.”

item.title: When Starshield Cut Out, Ukrainian Drones Fell From the Skies
item.description: New York Times: “Ukrainian accounts of Starshield’s abrupt throttling have become a flashpoint in a worsening feud between President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and President Trump. A week after the first problems were reported, Ukrainian troops said that the situation had improved but that connectivity issues remained. The Trump administration has offered mixed messages, both denying any change to Starshield service and saying that service has been restored.”

item.title: Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites
item.description: NiemanLab: “The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30. In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should ‘withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.'”

item.title: Trump Says Google CEO Rejected His Request to Rename Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps
item.description: Variety: “President Donald Trump, who has already renamed two bodies of water after America, said he would like to redub the Atlantic Ocean as well — but that the CEO of Google pushed back on the idea.”

item.title: A Vermont woman scrubs grime from gravestones and researches who is buried there
item.description: Associated Press: “[Caitlin] Abrams doesn’t solely focus on the cleaning process. She researches and then shares the details she has found of the individual lives in her videos while filming the moss and buildup being washed away. Abrams focuses on 18th and 19th century headstones in remote yet picturesque graveyards in Vermont, and her viewers are drawn to her deep dives into the past that also touch on the dark nature of death and spirits.”

item.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
item.description: CNBC: “Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company’s Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.”

item.title: California settles 23andMe data breach claims for $6 million
item.description: Reuters: “California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state will receive a $6 million settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s ​legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 ‌million customers’ genetic and other personal information.”

item.title: The Pentagon is quietly building an elite new tech sabotage agency
item.description: Politico: “The Pentagon has spent months quietly building an elite new tech agency to help covertly disrupt and sabotage foreign technology programs considered threats to American military superiority.”

item.title: Bye bye Alamy
item.description: Neil Turner Photographer: “The best that I could hope for was 40% but my calculations told me that I would be dropping to their basic 20% level pretty soon. I’m a level-headed chap and the thought that 20% of something is better than 100% of nothing went through my head many, many times. When you factor in that more and more of my limited sales were coming through at US$0.39 each and that I was actually only going to receive 8 US cents or around 6.5 British pennies for each of them, the final straw was well within reach.”

item.title: Nature beneath the power lines: Transforming utility corridors into public trails
item.description: Second Wave Media: “In Portage, partnerships with Consumers Energy have allowed land used for electricity infrastructure to become connections for bikers and pedestrians…. In July, Consumers Energy announced that it had not only surpassed its goal to ‘enhance, restore, or protect 6,500 acres of land,’ but reached that goal earlier than anticipated.” Good evening, Internet…
